events.additional_information: Third concert in the 'Cross Talk Tokyo' series of Japanese premieres of American and Japanese experimental/electronic music, co-sponsored by the American Cultural Center and the Asahi Newspaper Company. The program booklet also references 'Cross Talk 2' (an open rehearsal featuring Robert Ashley's 'in memoriam...Esteban Gomez' and Salvatore Martirano's 'Ballad', not otherwise detailed) and announces future plans for a winter 1968-69 live electronic music festival and spring 1969 'intermedia' events (Xenakis's Terretektorh, Cage's HPSCHD, and the premiere of Takemitsu's 'Flight-Operatic'), none of which are documented with performance details in this booklet. Substantial portions of this file consist of composer biography/program notes (partly duplicated in mirrored Japanese-language OCR text) rather than concert-listing data; these have been condensed rather than reproduced.

sections.additional_information: For brass quintet, film, and projections (film by David Freund and Larry Austin). Composer: Larry Austin. Marked as a First Japanese Performance. Conceived as a silent film accompanied by live electronic sound produced in real time by the performers (American Brass Quintet on the original recording) using electronically amplified mutes.
For 2 bassoons and percussion. Composer: Paul Chihara. Second in a series of 'tone pictures' dealing with trees, using chromatically tuned tenor drums as the principal sound source.

For cello, celesta, piano, percussion, and 4-channel amplification. Composer: Robert Morris. Marked as a First Japanese Performance. Uses indeterminacy as a structural device, with sounds arranged on a continuum from clear pitches to ambient noise.
For 2 string instruments. Composer: Akimichi Takeda. Marked as a World Premiere.

For flute, clarinet, violin, and cello. Composer: Milton Babbitt. Marked as a First Japanese Performance. The second of Babbitt's six 'Composition for...' works; twelve-tone serial, with temporal structure derived from the same principles as the pitch organization.

For string quartet, filters, and ring modulator. Composer: Yori-Aki Matsudaira. Marked as a World Premiere. Foreground string quartet combined with rear speakers emitting modulated products of the quartet's live sound; structured by mathematical distributions (Poisson, normal, etc.) applied to sound conditions.

Film with 4-channel electronic sound (film by Takahiko Iimura). Composer: Alvin Lucier. Marked as a First Japanese Performance. Collaboration between Lucier and filmmaker Iimura using scratched film, punched loops, and colored slides superimposed via three movie projectors and one slide projector, with sound from polarized vibrational pickups.

performances.performance_name: Sur la route de Côme à Milan, en 1815
performances.lyrics_transcript: Gendarmes stop a carriage carrying Fabrice del Dongo, a Napoleon admirer fleeing after Waterloo, and his young aunt the Countess Gina. A mix-up reveals the gendarmes were seeking General Conti and his daughter Clélia; on seeing Clélia, Fabrice falls deeply in love. Gina defuses a tense confrontation by offering the soldiers wine, and the party continues on.

performances.performance_name: Une loge, à la Scala de Milan
performances.lyrics_transcript: Days later, Gina and Milanese liberals discuss means of aiding Fabrice.

Fabrice, now at risk of imprisonment for killing a rival in a duel, takes refuge with Théodolinde; disguised as a peasant, he escapes by night, writing to Gina of his return and thinking still of Clélia.
performances.additional_information: Includes danced episodes choreographed by Albert Aveline.

performances.performance_name: La cour de la prison de Parme; the citadel
performances.lyrics_transcript: Fabrice is brought in chains to the citadel of Parma, where General Conti's faction triumphs over the Duchess's protégé; he strikes the jailer Barbone and is confined in the highest cell, 'Passive Obedience'. Clélia appears in a ball gown and the two are struck by each other. Later, with the guards drunk and Gina waiting below with a rope, Clélia urges Fabrice to escape; he resists, wishing to remain near her, until she threatens to enter a convent forever. After declaring their love, they part, and Clélia vows to the Madonna never to see Fabrice again if he escapes safely.

On Lake Maggiore, Fabrice pines for Clélia despite Gina's care. Mosca brings news: the Prince of Parme is dead, an insurrection has been mastered, and they may return to Parma — but Clélia is about to marry. Fabrice rushes off to reach her in time, while Mosca renews his declaration of love to the melancholy Gina.

Venues where such recitals had previously been given include the Royal College of Music, Trinity College of Music, and University of London; Edinburgh, Glasgow, Manchester, and Newcastle Universities; and the Oxford Summer School for Teachers.

performances.additional_information: Composer: P. I. Tchaikovsky. Performed by M. Bronislaw Huberman.

performances.lyrics_transcript: Lia laments the years passing without comfort, mourning her lost son Azaël; the return of spring only deepens her grief, and she recalls happy family evenings in the elm-planted plain, contrasting her sorrow with the joy of parents whose children remain.
performances.additional_information: Composer: C. Debussy, text by E. Guinand. Performed by Dame Nellie Melba.

performances.lyrics_transcript: Radamès dreams of being chosen to lead the army to victory and returning crowned with laurels to Aida, whom he praises as a heavenly, radiant beauty and wishes to restore to her native land and enthrone beside the sun.
performances.additional_information: Composer: G. Verdi. Performed by Mr. Tom Burke.

performances.performance_name: (a) Les Cloches; (b) Si mes vers avaient des ailes; (c) Aubade (Le Roi d'Ys); (d) Nymphes et Sylvains
performances.lyrics_transcript: (a) Bells ringing in a mild sky recall happy past years and the whiteness of altar flowers; (b) the poet wishes his verses had wings like a bird, like the spirit, like love, to fly to his beloved; (c) a lover vows to remain at his beloved's closed door forever, trusting her heart will soften; (d) nymphs and sylvans are called to dance in the woods through the night until dawn disperses them.
performances.additional_information: Composers: (a) C. Debussy; (b) Reynaldo Hahn; (c) É. Lalo; (d) H. Bemberg. Performed by Dame Nellie Melba.
Composers: (a) F. Schubert, arr. Wilhelmj; (b) N. Paganini. Performed by M. Bronislaw Huberman.

performances.lyrics_transcript: (a) A green leaf meets an early frost and is lost, a metaphor for youth spent too soon; (b) a farewell to summer, hope, and love, as leaves fall and swallows depart.
performances.additional_information: Composers: (a) Frank St. Leger; (b) F. P. Tosti (by special request). Performed by Dame Nellie Melba; encore: 'Comin' Thro' the Rye'.

performances.lyrics_transcript: (a) Flowers hold the memory of a beloved's voice and a kiss like fire; (b) a beloved who was once the singer's whole world is now only a lingering memory; (c) the Latin Ave Maria prayer.
performances.additional_information: Composers: (a) Goring Thomas; (b) Percy Kahn (accompanied by the composer), words by Alan Fenwick; (c) [setting unspecified]. Performed by Mr. Tom Burke.

performances.performance_name: O soave fanciulla ('Lovely Maid in the Moonlight'), Act I of La Bohème
performances.lyrics_transcript: Rodolfo praises Mimì as a vision in the moonlight; the two declare their love, and Mimì asks to accompany him rather than be left behind, ending in a shared cry of 'Amor!'
performances.additional_information: Composer: G. Puccini. Sung by special request. Mimì: Dame Nellie Melba; Rodolfo: Mr. Tom Burke.
